teaser: In 2016 you could sleep in this room for ten dollars a night. The real one was gone.
review_notes:
The image shows the Chicago version (second of three, September 1889): the two portraits at top right match it.
The 2016 Art Institute of Chicago Airbnb replica at 10 dollars a night: check.
Roy Lichtenstein's 'Bedroom at Arles' (1992): check.
Color change (walls and doors originally more violet, a red pigment having faded): based on technical studies of the versions; check wording for the Chicago canvas specifically.
The Yellow House damaged by bombing in 1944 and later demolished: check.
Left door leading to the guest room used by Gauguin: check.
The woman's portrait at top right is unidentified; the left one is generally read as a self-portrait.
Acquired by the Art Institute in 1926 (Helen Birch Bartlett Memorial Collection): check.

lesson.text: In 2016, a listing appeared on Airbnb: a small room in Chicago with blue walls, a wooden bed and two straw chairs, ten dollars a night. The Art Institute of Chicago had built this painting in three dimensions, crooked pictures included. The nights sold out within minutes.

The pop artist Roy Lichtenstein had already redone the room in 1992 in his comic-strip style, with tidy modern chairs. Few interiors in art are this familiar. And yet the canvas in Chicago is a copy, painted by Van Gogh from memory of a room he no longer lived in.

The room was real. In 1888 he rented four rooms in a small yellow house in Arles, in the south of France, and for the first time in his life he had a home of his own. He bought a bed, twelve chairs and a mirror, and in October he painted his bedroom to show his brother Theo what it looked like.

While Van Gogh was in the hospital in Arles, the Rhône river flooded and damp got into the Yellow House. The first Bedroom was damaged. Theo suggested he copy it before it was repaired, and that is why this second canvas exists.

He painted the copy in September 1889, a year after the original and in a very different place: the asylum of Saint-Rémy, where he had committed himself after a series of breakdowns. He set the damaged canvas beside a fresh one of the same size, about 72 by 91 cm (28 by 36 inches).

In his letters he explained what he was after. The picture should make you think of rest, of sleep in general. Color was to do everything. He listed each object with its color, as if dictating a recipe.
Go through the room the way his letter does, color by color.

spots.title: The bed
spots.text: He called it the yellow of fresh butter. It is enormous, heavy as a ship, and takes up a third of the canvas. He wanted furniture that looked solid and lasting.

spots.title: The red blanket
spots.text: One patch of scarlet in the whole room. Next to the greens and blues it glows hotter than it is: opposite colors, called complementaries, intensify each other.

spots.title: The window
spots.text: Green shutter frames, nearly closed, with yellow-green light behind the panes. There is no view. The outside world is shut out.

spots.title: The washstand
spots.text: A blue jug and basin, bottles and a glass on an orange-brown table. This is the whole of his toilet kit, lined up neatly.

lesson.title: A recipe in color

lesson.text: Notice what the colors do not have: shadows. No object darkens the floor beneath it. Van Gogh said he had left the shadows out on purpose, to paint in flat, clear tints like the Japanese woodblock prints he collected and pinned to his walls.

Some of the colors you see are not the ones he chose. He described the walls as pale violet. A red pigment in his mix has faded over the years, leaving them blue, so the room has shifted from the harmony he planned.

The thick paint is still exactly his. He applied it in short loaded strokes that stand up from the canvas, a technique called impasto. On the floor the strokes run in every direction, green over pink over gray, like worn boards scrubbed too often.
Above the bed hang the things that kept him company. In the first version, two of them were portraits of friends from Arles. For the copy painted in the asylum, he changed who was on the wall.
Van Gogh put himself in his own room. Where is his face?

spots.title: A self-portrait
spots.text: A man with reddish hair and beard on a green ground, hung at a tilt above the pillows. Beside him is a portrait of a woman whose identity is unknown. The friends from Arles are gone.

lesson.text: That small face changes the mood. In 1888 the walls spoke of friendship and of a house waiting for guests. A year later the friends had scattered, and the man looking down at the empty bed is the painter himself, alone with a memory.
The Bedroom is not a record of a room. It is a picture of what having a home meant to a man who had just lost it.

So is the room restful? Many viewers feel the opposite. The floor tips up, the bed's foot looms, the far wall seems to slide. Part of this is true to life: the room in the Yellow House really was an irregular shape, with one corner skewed. The rest is Van Gogh pressing everything close.

spots.title: The near chair
spots.text: A plain straw-seated chair, cut by the left edge. It stands almost on your feet, as if you had just come through the door.

spots.title: The second chair
spots.text: Pulled up by the bed and facing it. Two chairs, two pillows, one occupant: the room is furnished for company that is absent.

spots.title: The mirror
spots.text: A black-framed mirror hangs by the window and reflects only pale light. No face appears in it: the room is shown without its occupant.

spots.title: Clothes on pegs
spots.text: His blue work jackets hang from a rail behind the bed, and at the right end sits his straw hat.

spots.title: The landscape
spots.text: A small painting of a tree in a field, hung from a nail by a triangle of cord. Even on his bedroom wall he hung the countryside.

spots.title: The towel
spots.text: A striped towel hangs from a nail by the door. Its red stripes echo the blanket across the room.

spots.title: The floor
spots.text: No two strokes agree. He wrote of red floor tiles, but here the floor has turned greenish gray with pink showing through.

spots.title: The door on the left
spots.text: One of two doors that frame the picture. This one led to the guest room he prepared for the painter Paul Gauguin, who stayed two months.

lesson.text: The Yellow House itself did not survive. It was damaged by bombs in 1944, during the Second World War, and was later pulled down. The bedroom now exists only in paint.

He painted it a third time that same month, smaller, as a gift for his mother and sister. That one is in Paris, the first is in Amsterdam, and this one reached Chicago in 1926. Three cities each own the room, and when the Art Institute needed a fourth for its guests, it had to build it from the painting.

quiz.question: Why did Van Gogh paint a second version of his bedroom?
options: The first had been damaged by damp after a flood
quiz.explanation: The first canvas was damaged and Theo suggested copying it.

quiz.question: Where was he when he painted the Chicago version?
options: In the Yellow House in Arles
quiz.explanation: He painted it in September 1889 at Saint-Rémy.

quiz.question: Why are there no shadows in the room?
options: It is meant to be night
He left them out to imitate Japanese prints
quiz.explanation: He wanted flat clear tints like the prints he collected.

quiz.question: What did he say the picture should suggest?
quiz.explanation: His letters say color should suggest rest or sleep.

quiz.question: Whose portrait hangs above the bed in this version?
quiz.explanation: He replaced a friend's portrait with a self-portrait.

quiz.question: What happened to the walls' color over time?
options: They were repainted by a restorer
A red pigment faded, turning violet into blue
quiz.explanation: He described the walls as pale violet; the red component has faded.

facts.text: The Yellow House in Arles can still be visited today.
facts.explanation: It was bombed in 1944 and later demolished.

facts.text: Van Gogh painted three versions of the Bedroom.
facts.explanation: They are in Amsterdam, Chicago and Paris.

facts.text: The Chicago canvas was painted in the bedroom itself.
facts.explanation: It was copied from the first version at the asylum of Saint-Rémy.
